glazelite

Fast JSON reading and writing for R, built on the Glaze C++ library.

glazelite offers the familiar toJSON() / fromJSON() interface of jsonlite for the common cases, with the encoding and parsing done by Glaze, a header-only C++23 library by Stephen Berry.

  • Familiar. The same function names, arguments and output as jsonlite (see A substitute for jsonlite).
  • Fast. Typically 5 to 10 times faster than jsonlite for vectors and data frames, and far more for nested lists (see Performance).
  • Streams to disk. write_json() and stream_out() write incrementally, so a document can be larger than a single R string, which is limited to 2 GB.
  • Exact numbers. Doubles are written with full round-trip precision.
  • Strict input. Truncated documents and trailing content are errors, not partial results.

Installation 

# once the package is on CRAN
install.packages("glazelite")

# development version from GitHub
# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("ninohardt/glazelite")

Building from source needs R 4.3.0 or later and a C++23 compiler; upstream Glaze currently tests with GCC 13+ and Clang 19+.

Usage

Convert R objects to JSON and back 

library(glazelite)

toJSON(list(id = 1L, tags = c("a", "b"), ok = TRUE), auto_unbox = TRUE)
#> {"id":1,"tags":["a","b"],"ok":true}

df <- data.frame(id = 1:2, name = c("Ada", "Grace"), score = c(9.5, NA))
toJSON(df)
#> [{"id":1,"name":"Ada","score":9.5},{"id":2,"name":"Grace"}]

toJSON(df, dataframe = "columns", pretty = TRUE)
#> {
#>   "id": [1, 2],
#>   "name": ["Ada", "Grace"],
#>   "score": [9.5, null]
#> }

toJSON(array(1:8, c(2, 2, 2)))
#> [[[1,5],[3,7]],[[2,6],[4,8]]]

Arrays of records come back as data frames, and arrays of scalars as vectors:

fromJSON('[{"id":1,"name":"Ada","score":9.5},{"id":2,"name":"Grace"}]')
#>   id  name score
#> 1  1   Ada   9.5
#> 2  2 Grace    NA

str(fromJSON('{"id": 1, "tags": ["a", "b"], "nested": {"ok": true, "x": [1.5, null]}}'))
#> List of 3
#>  $ id    : int 1
#>  $ tags  : chr [1:2] "a" "b"
#>  $ nested:List of 2
#>   ..$ ok: logi TRUE
#>   ..$ x : num [1:2] 1.5 NA

Read and write files 

path <- tempfile(fileext = ".json")
write_json(df, path)
read_json(path)
#>   id  name score
#> 1  1   Ada   9.5
#> 2  2 Grace    NA

write_json() writes to a temporary file next to path and moves it into place when it is complete, so a failed write never leaves a damaged file.

Stream newline-delimited JSON

stream_out() writes one record per line from a data frame, a list of records, or a function that returns one batch at a time and finally NULL:

ndjson <- tempfile(fileext = ".ndjson")
i <- 0L
stream_out(function() {
  i <<- i + 1L
  if (i > 3L) return(NULL)
  data.frame(batch = i, value = c(0.5, 1.5))
}, ndjson)

readLines(ndjson, n = 2)
#> [1] "{\"batch\":1,\"value\":0.5}" "{\"batch\":1,\"value\":1.5}"

stream_in(ndjson)
#>   batch value
#> 1     1   0.5
#> 2     1   1.5
#> 3     2   0.5
#> 4     2   1.5
#> 5     3   0.5
#> 6     3   1.5

Pass a handler to stream_in() to process the file page by page without holding all of it in memory:

total <- 0
stream_in(ndjson, handler = function(page) total <<- total + sum(page$value),
          pagesize = 2)
total
#> [1] 6

Performance

Median of seven runs in seconds on one Windows 10 machine (R 4.5.2, GCC 14.2, glazelite 0.1.2, yyjsonr 0.1.22, jsonlite 2.0.0), converting in memory with toJSON() / fromJSON() and their counterparts. jsonlite was called with digits = NA. Treat the numbers as indicative only.

Task glazelite yyjsonr jsonlite
Write 1e6 doubles 0.09 0.07 0.86
Write 1000 x 1000 double matrix 0.09 0.08 0.93
Write data frame, 2e5 rows x 6 0.17 0.11 0.81
Write nested list, 2e4 records 0.02 0.02 5.69
Read 1e6 doubles 0.08 0.03 0.94
Read data frame, 2e5 rows x 6 0.25 0.11 1.53
Read nested list, 2e4 records 0.04 0.01 0.30

yyjsonr is faster still, particularly for reading.

A substitute for jsonlite

glazelite keeps jsonlite’s function names, argument names and output. For the common cases, replacing library(jsonlite) with library(glazelite) is all that is needed, and the JSON that is written stays the same. The package’s tests compare its output with jsonlite’s for vectors, arrays of every shape and all data frame layouts.

yyjsonr, the fastest JSON package for R, makes a different trade-off: it has its own interface (write_json_str(), read_json_str(), options objects), and what it writes differs from jsonlite in places. With default options (jsonlite with digits = NA, yyjsonr 0.1.22):

R object jsonlite and glazelite yyjsonr
c(1.5, 2) [1.5,2] [1.5,2.0]
array(1:4) [1,2,3,4] error
array(1:12, c(2, 3, 2)) [[[1,7],[3,9],[5,11]],[[2,8],[4,10],[6,12]]] [[[1,3,5],[2,4,6]],[[7,9,11],[8,10,12]]]
array(1:16, c(2, 2, 2, 2)) four nested levels error: more than three dimensions
array(integer(), c(2, 0, 3)) [[],[]] [[[],[]],[[],[]],[[],[]]]
data frame with a 2 x 2 matrix column m [{"id":1,"m":[1,3]},{"id":2,"m":[2,4]}] [{"id":1,"m":1},{"id":2,"m":2}]
data.frame(id = 1:2, v = c(NA, 2.5)) [{"id":1},{"id":2,"v":2.5}] [{"id":1,"v":null},{"id":2,"v":2.5}]

glazelite does not cover all of jsonlite yet. The differences that remain:

Writing

  • Supported inputs are logical, integer, double, character, and factor vectors; arrays of any dimension; lists; and data frames of those types, including matrix, list, and data-frame columns. Other classes, such as dates and date-times, and complex and raw vectors raise an error instead of being converted; jsonlite and yyjsonr write dates as strings.
  • The dataframe, auto_unbox, na, factor, always_decimal, and pretty options are implemented. digits must be NA: numbers always keep full precision, and rounding is not implemented.
  • Missing values are written as null by default (na = "string" writes "NA"). In the row layout of a data frame, missing fields are omitted, as in jsonlite.
  • Arrays keep their dimension order and dimensions of length one or zero. As with jsonlite, auto_unbox = TRUE keeps dimensioned length-one vectors and values wrapped in I() as JSON arrays.
  • Factors are written as labels; factor = "integer" writes their level indices. always_decimal = TRUE keeps a decimal point or exponent for doubles, while integers and factor codes stay integers.

Reading

  • Arrays of scalars of one type become atomic vectors, and arrays of records with scalar fields become data frames.
  • There is no matrix simplification: [[1,2],[3,4]] becomes a list of two vectors, where jsonlite and yyjsonr return a matrix.
  • Arrays of mixed types stay lists instead of being coerced to character, and records with nested fields stay lists of records.

Large files

toJSON() returns one R string and therefore cannot exceed R’s string limit. write_json() and stream_out() do not have that limit: values are split and flushed to the file through an output buffer of about 64 KiB, including pretty-printed output. The R object being written must still fit in memory; with stream_out() a generated batch need not be kept once it is written.

On a Linux development machine, a batch generator wrote an NDJSON file of 2,181,230,740 bytes in 7.86 seconds with a peak process memory of about 64 MiB.

read_json() avoids loading the file as an R string, but the parsed result still occupies R memory.

Credits

All JSON encoding and parsing is done by Glaze, a header-only C++ library by Stephen Berry, licensed under the MIT license. Glaze in turn contains code from fast_float (Daniel Lemire, João Paulo Magalhaes and contributors), zmij (Victor Zverovich) and a constexpr xxh64 implementation (Daniel Kirchner). Copyright holders and licenses are listed in inst/COPYRIGHTS.

The bundled Glaze headers are pinned to commit c5ed7ddc249a2c3d15ede60f985adf447aa11ed3 under inst/include/glaze. Only the headers needed for JSON are included, and pragmas that suppress compiler diagnostics are removed to comply with CRAN policy; tools/vendor-glaze.R reproduces both steps from a Glaze checkout.
